title: Hinduism and Buddhism: Dharma, Karma, Awakening
bigQuestion: How do Hindu and Buddhist traditions explain why people suffer and how a person can find freedom?

story.title: The King Who Carved His Regret
story.kicker: After a bloody war, an Indian emperor did something few rulers do: he said he was sorry, in stone.
paragraphs: In about 261 BCE, the armies of the emperor Ashoka marched into Kalinga, a land on the east coast of India. Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire, which stretched across most of the Indian subcontinent. His soldiers won. The cost was enormous. Ashoka's own words later said that about 100,000 people were killed and about 150,000 were carried away as captives.

Ashoka did not celebrate. Instead, he ordered words carved on rocks and tall stone pillars across his empire. In one of these messages, called Rock Edict XIII, the king says he feels deep sorrow over Kalinga. He writes that the only true conquest is a conquest by dhamma, a word that here means right conduct and moral teaching.

The edicts ask people to respect their parents, to be kind to servants and to animals, and to honor the teachers of every religious group. Ashoka had become a follower of the Buddha's teaching. Yet he urged respect for all sects, not only his own. His messages were written in local languages and scripts so ordinary people could hear them read aloud.

Some of these pillars still stand today. One pillar top, with four lions standing back to back, became the national emblem of modern India. Historians still debate how Ashoka governed after Kalinga. But his carved words remain one of the oldest records of a ruler trying to rule by a moral teaching.
story.think: Why might a powerful king choose to carve his regret in public, where everyone could read it?

lessons.title: The Vedas and the Upanishads
lessons.mainIdea: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, and the Upanishads within them explore the link between the self and ultimate reality.
reading: Before sunrise in many Hindu homes, someone chants a short verse in Sanskrit called the Gayatri Mantra. It comes from the Rig Veda, one of the oldest texts still used in worship anywhere. Hindus call these texts the *Vedas*, from a Sanskrit word meaning knowledge. There are four Vedas, and many Hindus regard them as revealed truth that ancient sages heard, not wrote.

Scholars date the oldest parts of the Rig Veda to about 1500 to 1200 BCE. For centuries, the Vedas were passed on by memory. Priests trained for years to chant every sound exactly. Only much later were they written down. The Vedas contain hymns to many deities, instructions for fire rituals and, in their later parts, deep questions about life.

Those later parts are the *Upanishads*, composed from about 800 BCE onward. They ask: What is the real self? What is behind all things? Many Upanishads answer that the inner self, called Atman, is one with Brahman, the ultimate reality. Hindu schools of thought read this teaching in different ways, and they still debate it today.

words.d: the four oldest Hindu scriptures, first passed on by memory in Sanskrit
later texts of the Vedas that explore the self and ultimate reality
in Hindu thought, the true inner self

look.title: A Father Teaches His Son
look.text: A father asks his son to put salt into water overnight. In the morning the son cannot find the salt, yet every sip tastes salty. The father explains that the finest essence is present in everything in the same way, unseen. That essence is the true self. And, he tells his son, you are that.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (the teaching of Uddalaka to Shvetaketu), paraphrase
look.prompt: What does the salt stand for in the father's lesson? What is he trying to help his son understand about himself?

check.q: What does the word Veda mean?
check.why: Veda comes from a Sanskrit word for knowledge. Duty is dharma; rebirth is part of samsara.

check.q: How were the Vedas passed on for many centuries?
check.why: Priests memorized and chanted the Vedas exactly; writing came much later. Stone pillars belong to Ashoka.

check.q: What question is at the center of the Upanishads?
choices: the link between the inner self and ultimate reality
check.why: The Upanishads explore Atman, the inner self, and Brahman, ultimate reality.

lessons.title: Two Great Epics
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are long story-poems that teach Hindus about duty through heroes facing hard choices.
reading: Every autumn, in towns across northern India, actors perform the story of Prince Rama. Crowds watch him lose his throne, go into the forest with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana, and rescue Sita from the demon king Ravana. This story is the *Ramayana*, an epic poem traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki. Many Hindus see Rama as an image of perfect duty and honor.

The *Mahabharata* is even longer. Scholars call it one of the longest poems ever composed, with about 100,000 verses in its fullest form. It tells of a great war between two branches of one royal family. Both epics grew over many centuries, roughly between 400 BCE and 400 CE. Today many families know them through retellings, comics and TV series.

Inside the Mahabharata is the *Bhagavad Gita*, or Song of the Lord. Just before battle, the warrior Arjuna does not want to fight his own relatives. His charioteer, Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as a form of God, teaches him. Krishna says Arjuna must do his duty without being attached to the results. Hindus have read this teaching in many ways, and millions study it closely.

words.d: a Hindu epic poem about Prince Rama, Sita and the rescue from Ravana
a very long Hindu epic about a war between two branches of one family
a part of the Mahabharata in which Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna

look.title: Krishna Speaks to Arjuna
look.text: You have a right to do your work, but not to its fruits. Do not let the reward be your reason for acting, and do not fall into doing nothing. Act with a steady mind, the same in success and failure.
look.prompt: Krishna tells Arjuna to act without being attached to results. How could a student use this idea while studying for a test?

check.q: Who is the hero of the Ramayana?
check.why: The Ramayana tells of Prince Rama. Arjuna is a warrior in the Mahabharata.

check.q: Where is the Bhagavad Gita found?
check.why: The Gita is a section of the Mahabharata, set just before its great battle.

check.q: In the Gita, what does Krishna urge Arjuna to do?
choices: leave home and become a monk
do his duty without clinging to the results
check.why: Krishna teaches action without attachment to its fruits (Gita 2.47).

lessons.title: Brahman and the Deities
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus worship many deities while understanding them as forms or faces of one ultimate reality, Brahman.
reading: Walk into a Hindu temple and you may see many sacred images, called murtis. One shows Ganesha, with an elephant's head, whom many Hindus pray to before starting something new. Another shows Lakshmi, linked with good fortune. Another shows Shiva, dancing in a ring of fire. A visitor might ask: how many gods do Hindus worship?

Hindus answer in different ways. Many describe one ultimate reality, *Brahman*, beyond all names and forms. They see the many *deities* as forms or faces of that one reality. A common saying from the Rig Veda states that truth is one, but the wise call it by many names. Other Hindus focus devotion on one supreme God, such as Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess, called Devi.

Families often have an ishta devata, a chosen deity they feel closest to. Followers of Vishnu are called Vaishnavas. Followers of Shiva are called Shaivas. Followers of the Goddess are called Shaktas. These are not separate religions. They are major paths within Hinduism, and they share many texts, festivals and ideas.

words.d: in Hindu thought, the one ultimate reality behind all things
gods and goddesses who are worshiped
a sacred image of a deity used in Hindu worship

look.title: One Reality, Many Names
look.text: A Hindu grandmother keeps a small shrine at home with images of Ganesha, Krishna and Lakshmi. Her grandson asks if she believes in three gods. She says each one shows her a different face of the same divine reality, like one person who is a mother, a teacher and a friend.
look.prompt: Use the words Brahman and deities to explain the grandmother's answer in your own words.

check.q: What is Brahman in Hindu thought?
choices: the one ultimate reality behind all things
check.why: Brahman is the ultimate reality; many Hindus see the deities as its forms.

check.q: A family prays to Ganesha before starting a new business. Why?
choices: Ganesha is the hero of the Ramayana
many Hindus pray to Ganesha before new beginnings
check.why: Many Hindus honor Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity, at the start of new work.

check.q: What is a Vaishnava?
choices: a Hindu whose devotion centers on Vishnu
check.why: Vaishnavas focus devotion on Vishnu; followers of Shiva are Shaivas.

lessons.title: Dharma, Karma, Samsara, Moksha
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu teaching links duty, the results of actions, the cycle of rebirth and the hope of release into one picture of life.
reading: A teenager in Chennai helps care for her grandfather, studies hard and tells the truth even when it costs her. Her family might say she is following her *dharma*. Dharma means duty, or the right way to live. In Hindu teaching, a person's dharma depends partly on their stage of life and role, such as student, parent or elder.

Hindus teach that every action has results that return to the one who acts. This is *karma*. Good actions tend to bring good results; harmful actions bring suffering. Many Hindus believe karma carries across lifetimes. The soul is reborn again and again in a cycle called *samsara*, and karma helps shape each new birth.

The highest goal, many Hindus say, is *moksha*, release from the cycle of rebirth. Hindu paths describe different ways toward moksha. The path of knowledge seeks insight. The path of devotion seeks loving surrender to God. The path of action does one's duty selflessly. Many Hindus combine these paths in daily life.

words.d: duty; the right way to live for one's role and stage of life
the teaching that actions bring results back to the one who acts
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
in Hindu teaching, release from the cycle of rebirth

look.title: Four Words, One Circle
look.text: Picture a wheel. On the rim are the words birth, life, death and rebirth. Arrows labeled karma push the wheel around. A path labeled dharma runs along the rim. At the center, off the wheel, is a doorway labeled moksha.
look.prompt: Explain what each part of the picture stands for in Hindu teaching. Why is moksha drawn off the wheel?

check.q: Which word means the cycle of birth, death and rebirth?
check.why: Samsara is the cycle of rebirth; moksha is release from it.

check.q: A man keeps his promises and cares for his family because it is his duty. Which Hindu idea fits best?
check.why: Dharma is duty or the right way to live.

check.q: What do many Hindus see as the highest goal?
check.why: Many Hindus describe moksha as the final goal beyond samsara.

lessons.title: Puja, Temples and Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu worship happens at home and in temples through offerings, prayers and festivals that bring families together.
reading: In the morning, a mother in Aurora, Illinois, rings a small bell at the family shrine. She offers a flower, lights a lamp and waves it in circles before an image of Krishna. This act of worship is called *puja*. Puja can be simple or grand. It often includes light, flowers, food, incense and prayer.

In a *mandir*, or Hindu temple, priests care for the murtis each day, bathing and dressing them. Worshipers come for darshan, which means seeing and being seen by the deity. The Chicago area has several large temples. The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago in Lemont and the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora draw families from across the region.

Festivals mark the Hindu year, which follows a lunar calendar. *Diwali*, the festival of lights, comes in October or November. Families light lamps, share sweets and, for many, honor Lakshmi or remember Rama's return home. Holi, in spring, is known for throwing bright colored powder. Other festivals honor Ganesha, Durga and Krishna.

words.d: Hindu worship with offerings such as light, flowers and food
a Hindu temple
the Hindu festival of lights, in October or November

look.title: Where Hindus Live
look.cite: Rounded common estimates from recent census and survey data; estimates vary
look.prompt: About what share of the world's Hindus live in India? What does this tell you about where Hinduism grew?

check.q: What is puja?
choices: worship with offerings such as light and flowers
check.why: Puja is Hindu worship, at home or in a mandir.

check.q: Which festival is known as the festival of lights?
check.why: Diwali is the festival of lights. Holi is the festival of colors; Vesak is Buddhist.

check.q: According to the data, where do most of the world's Hindus live?
check.why: About 1.1 billion Hindus live in India, far more than anywhere else.

lessons.title: Caste: History and Reform
lessons.mainIdea: Caste was a social ranking system in India; many reformers, Hindu and others, worked to end discrimination based on it.
reading: Ancient texts describe four social groups called *varnas*: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, merchants and farmers, and laborers. Over time, society in India also divided into thousands of smaller birth groups called jatis. People often married inside their group and did work linked to it. Scholars call this whole system *caste*.

Some groups were treated as outside the system and called untouchable. They faced harsh exclusion from temples, wells and schools. Many Hindu reformers rejected this treatment, citing the teaching that the same divine self lives in every person. Mahatma Gandhi campaigned against untouchability. Many people today use the name Dalit for these communities.

B. R. Ambedkar, born into a Dalit family, became a lawyer and led the writing of India's Constitution. It took effect in 1950 and outlawed untouchability. In 1956, Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of followers became Buddhists, seeking a path without caste. Discrimination based on caste has not fully disappeared, and Indians still debate how best to end it.

words.d: a system of social groups based on birth, historically linked to work and marriage
one of four broad social groups described in ancient Indian texts
a name many people use for communities once treated as untouchable

look.title: Two Responses to Caste
look.text: Gandhi stayed a Hindu and worked to reform Hindu practice from within, calling for temples to open to everyone. Ambedkar decided that leaving Hinduism for Buddhism was the better path for his followers. Both men wanted to end discrimination based on birth.
look.prompt: Compare the two responses. What did each man believe would bring change? Describe both without judging either.

check.q: What did India's Constitution of 1950 do?
check.why: The 1950 Constitution, led by Ambedkar, outlawed untouchability.

check.q: Why did Ambedkar become a Buddhist in 1956?
choices: he sought a path without caste
he wanted to become a king
check.why: Ambedkar and his followers chose Buddhism as a path free of caste ranking.

check.q: What are jatis?
choices: thousands of smaller birth groups in Indian society
check.why: Jatis are many smaller birth groups; varnas are the four broad groups.

lessons.title: Siddhartha Becomes the Buddha
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist tradition tells how Prince Siddhartha left a life of comfort to seek an end to suffering and became the Buddha, the awakened one.
reading: Buddhist tradition tells of a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, born in Lumbini, in what is now Nepal. Scholars often place his life in the 5th century BCE, though dates vary. His father kept him inside the palace, surrounded by comfort. According to the story, on trips outside he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a calm wandering holy man.

Troubled, Siddhartha left home to seek an answer to suffering. For years he tried extreme fasting, but it did not bring the answer. He chose a *Middle Way* between luxury and harsh self-denial. Seated under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he meditated until, Buddhists say, he reached awakening. From then on he was called the *Buddha*, which means awakened one.

The Buddha taught for about 45 years across northern India. He gathered a *sangha*, a community of monks and nuns, and lay followers. Buddhists call the Buddha, his teaching (the Dharma) and the Sangha the Three Jewels. Many Buddhists recite that they take refuge in these three.

words.d: the awakened one; the title given to Siddhartha Gautama
the Buddha's path between too much comfort and harsh self-denial
the Buddhist community, especially of monks and nuns

look.title: The First Verse of the Dhammapada
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 1, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: The Dhammapada is a collection of sayings Buddhists credit to the Buddha. What does this verse say about the power of the mind?

check.q: What does the title Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha means awakened one, the title given to Siddhartha after his awakening.

check.q: What is the Middle Way?
choices: a path between luxury and harsh self-denial
check.why: After trying extreme fasting, Siddhartha chose a Middle Way between extremes.

check.q: Which are the Three Jewels of Buddhism?
choices: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha
the Vedas, the Gita and the Upanishads
check.why: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, his teaching and the community.

lessons.title: Four Truths and an Eightfold Path
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach that suffering has a cause and an end, and that the Eightfold Path is the way to reach that end, called nirvana.
reading: Buddhist tradition says the Buddha's first sermon took place in a deer park near Varanasi. There he taught the *Four Noble Truths*. First, life involves suffering, or dukkha, a word that also means dissatisfaction. Second, suffering comes from craving, which means wanting and clinging. Third, suffering can end. Fourth, there is a path that leads to its end.

That path is the *Eightfold Path*: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Buddhists often group these into three parts: wisdom, ethical conduct and meditation. Here right means wise or skillful, not a rule to obey out of fear.

The goal is *nirvana*, a word that means blowing out, as a flame is blown out. Buddhists describe it as the end of craving and suffering and freedom from rebirth. Like Hindus, Buddhists speak of karma and rebirth. But the Buddha taught that there is no permanent, unchanging self. This is one key point where Buddhist and Hindu teachings differ.

words.d: the Buddha's teaching on suffering, its cause, its end and the path
the eight practices Buddhists follow to end suffering
in Buddhism, the end of craving and suffering and freedom from rebirth

look.title: The First Sermon
look.text: This is the truth of suffering: birth, aging, sickness and death are suffering. This is its cause: craving, which leads to rebirth. This is its ending: the complete fading away of that craving. And this is the path that leads to its ending: the Noble Eightfold Path.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion), Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, paraphrase
look.prompt: Doctors name an illness, find its cause, say whether it can be cured and prescribe a treatment. How does the first sermon follow the same order?

check.q: According to the Four Noble Truths, what causes suffering?
check.why: The Second Noble Truth names craving, or clinging, as the cause of suffering.

check.q: What does nirvana mean literally?
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out, like a flame; duty is dharma and knowledge is veda.

check.q: On which point do Buddhist and Hindu teachings differ?
choices: Buddhists teach there is no permanent self
check.why: Both speak of karma and rebirth, but the Buddha taught no permanent self, while many Hindus speak of Atman.

lessons.title: Ashoka and the Silk Road
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism spread from India across Asia through rulers like Ashoka, monks, pilgrims and traders on the Silk Road.
reading: Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire from about 268 to 232 BCE. After the war in Kalinga, he supported the Buddha's teaching. His *edicts*, carved on rocks and pillars, urged kindness, honesty and respect for all religious groups. According to Buddhist tradition, he sent teachers far and wide, and his son Mahinda carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

Over the following centuries, monks and merchants traveled along the *Silk Road*, the network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India. Buddhism reached China by about the 1st century CE. From China it spread to Korea and then to Japan by the 6th century CE. It also traveled by sea to Southeast Asia.

Pilgrims carried texts home. The Chinese monk Xuanzang walked to India in the 600s CE and returned with hundreds of Buddhist texts to translate. In Afghanistan, huge statues of the Buddha were carved into the cliffs at Bamiyan. Each new land shaped Buddhism, blending it with local languages, art and customs.

words.d: an official public order or message from a ruler
a network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India
a person who travels to a holy place for religious reasons

look.title: Ashoka's Regret
look.text: After Kalinga was conquered, the king felt deep sorrow for the killing, death and captivity of so many people. He now holds that the best conquest is conquest by dhamma, and he honors all sects and wishes them to grow in their essential teaching.
look.cite: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (c. 256 BCE), paraphrase
look.prompt: How does Ashoka describe a better kind of conquest? What does he ask of the different religious groups?

check.q: How did Ashoka share his message across his empire?
choices: by carving edicts on rocks and pillars
check.why: Ashoka's edicts were carved on rocks and pillars; the first sermon was the Buddha's.

check.q: What was the Silk Road?
choices: a network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India
check.why: Monks and traders carried Buddhism along these trade routes.

check.q: Why did Xuanzang travel to India?
choices: to gather Buddhist texts to bring back to China
check.why: The monk Xuanzang brought hundreds of texts back to China to translate.

lessons.title: Theravada, Mahayana and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism grew into major branches, including Theravada and Mahayana, and today Buddhists of many branches live in Chicago.
reading: In Thailand, young men in saffron robes walk barefoot at dawn while families place rice in their bowls. This is *Theravada* Buddhism, meaning the Teaching of the Elders. It is common in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia. Theravada Buddhists use scriptures in the Pali language and give monks a central role.

*Mahayana*, meaning Great Vehicle, spread in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Mahayana teaching honors the *bodhisattva*, a being who seeks awakening in order to help all others. Mahayana includes Pure Land practice, which centers on devotion to Amida Buddha, and Zen, which stresses meditation. Tibetan Buddhism, sometimes called Vajrayana, is another major tradition.

At Chicago's World's Parliament of Religions in 1893, the Sri Lankan teacher Anagarika Dharmapala spoke for Buddhism. Today the Chicago area has temples of many Buddhist traditions. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago, in Uptown, was founded in 1944 by Japanese Americans. Thai, Vietnamese, Tibetan and Zen communities worship across the city and suburbs.

words.d: the Teaching of the Elders; the Buddhist branch common in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
the Great Vehicle; the Buddhist branch common in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam
in Mahayana Buddhism, a being who seeks awakening to help all others

look.title: The World's Largest Traditions
look.cite: Rounded common estimates of world religious populations; estimates vary
look.prompt: About how many times more Hindus than Buddhists are there? Why might counting Buddhists be harder in countries where people follow more than one tradition?

check.q: Which branch of Buddhism is common in Thailand and Sri Lanka?
check.why: Theravada, the Teaching of the Elders, is the main branch in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

check.q: What is a bodhisattva?
choices: a being who seeks awakening to help all others
check.why: The bodhisattva ideal is central to Mahayana Buddhism.

check.q: Who spoke for Buddhism at Chicago's 1893 Parliament of Religions?
check.why: Dharmapala, from Sri Lanka, represented Buddhism at the 1893 Parliament.

review.q: Which texts are the oldest Hindu scriptures?
review.why: The Vedas, with parts dating to about 1500 BCE, are the oldest Hindu scriptures.

review.q: In the Bhagavad Gita, who teaches Arjuna?
review.why: Krishna, Arjuna's charioteer, teaches him in the Gita.

review.q: Many Hindus describe the deities as forms of what?
review.why: Many Hindus see the deities as faces of Brahman.

review.q: Which pair of ideas do Hindus and Buddhists share?
choices: the Four Noble Truths and the Vedas
review.why: Both traditions speak of karma and rebirth, though they explain them differently.

review.q: What is the goal of the Eightfold Path?
review.why: Buddhists follow the Eightfold Path toward nirvana.

review.q: After the Kalinga war, what did Ashoka call the best conquest?
review.why: In Rock Edict XIII, Ashoka calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest.

review.q: Which branch of Buddhism honors the bodhisattva ideal and includes Zen?
review.why: Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana traditions; Vaishnava and Shaiva are Hindu paths.

review.q: Who led the writing of India's Constitution and later became a Buddhist?
review.why: Ambedkar led the Constitution's drafting and became a Buddhist in 1956.
